name: Voyager 2
significance: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune, and with them it completed a 'Grand Tour' of all four giant planets that a rare lining-up of the planets made possible once every 175 years. Launched first, two weeks before its twin, it reached Jupiter in July 1979 and saw Io's volcanoes still erupting four months after Voyager 1 discovered them, along with a much closer view of Europa's strangely smooth, cracked ice. At Saturn in 1981 it mapped the rings in finer detail. At Uranus in January 1986 it found ten new moons, a magnetic field tilted far off the planet's spin axis and off its centre, and Miranda, a small moon with a jumbled patchwork of terrains unlike anything seen before. At Neptune in August 1989 it found a Great Dark Spot, the fastest winds measured on any planet at the time, and on the moon Triton, the coldest surface yet measured, plumes of nitrogen erupting from the ice. It is still sending data from interstellar space.
statusNote: Launched 1977-08-20 14:29:44 UT on a Titan IIIE-Centaur from Cape Canaveral (Siddiqi, Beyond Earth; NSSDCA 1977-076A agrees on the date). Closest approaches (NSSDC Voyager table, UTC at the spacecraft): Jupiter 1979-07-09 22:29:51 at 10.11 Jupiter radii (about 722,000 km from the centre); Saturn 1981-08-26 03:24:57 at 2.67 Saturn radii (about 161,000 km); Uranus 1986-01-24 17:59:47 at 4.19 Uranus radii (about 107,000 km; 81,500 km above the cloud tops, Siddiqi); Neptune 1989-08-25 03:56:36 at 1.18 Neptune radii (about 29,200 km; 4,800 km above the cloud tops, Siddiqi). Moon flybys: Europa 205,720 km and Miranda 28,260 km (Siddiqi); Triton about 39,700 km from its centre (Horizons). Siddiqi gives Saturn's closest approach as 01:21 UT; NSSDC's table and Horizons both give 03:24 UT, which is used. Contact continues: Voyager 2 crossed the termination shock on 2007-08-30 (NASA; Siddiqi) and the heliopause into interstellar space on 2018-11-05 (NASA). TRAJECTORY: JPL Horizons target -32. Horizons' header describes 1977-08-20 to 1989-08-29 as "a patched conic mission-design type trajectory in which the conics were constructed to approximately match specific events (such satellite encounters), providing a rough accuracy", and the trajectory after that as a 2022 refit of the 1989-1992 tracking data by R. Jacobson (former Voyager navigation). Horizons is the primary source here, and its planet encounters agree with NSSDC's published closest approaches within about 0.3% (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune), so the path is drawn solid. The heliocentric path is Lambert legs between Horizons positions, with planet-centred tours at Jupiter and Saturn (tools/build_voyager.py, tools/build_planet_tour.py); Uranus and Neptune tours too, with the Miranda (1986-01-24 17:02, 28,000 km altitude) and Triton (1989-08-25 09:10, 38,400 km altitude) flybys, within 200 km of Horizons. The path stops where Voyager 2 passes 54.514 AU from the Sun, 1.1 times Pluto's farthest distance (its aphelion, 49.558 AU), on 1998-04-09: past that it is out of the Solar System view until a heliosphere layer is added (docs/outer-missions-plan.md section 1). BEYOND THE SOLAR SYSTEM VIEW: the heliosphere layer (zoom out past the Solar System view, or 'Open heliosphere view') draws the path on from the cutoff to 2050, from JPL Horizons (heliospherePath): solid to 2026-11-27, while the craft is still in contact, and dashed after, as a projection. Horizons describes this part of its trajectory as a "Refit of tracking data spanning 1989-1992 (from Neptune encounter to the end of two-way coherent transponder data). Produced in 2022 by R. Jacobson (former Voyager navigation) using DE440 to generate a new solution and long-term prediction." No two-way tracking has been possible since 1992, so the positions since then are that solution's prediction; they're drawn solid because Horizons is the primary source and the craft is still in contact. On 2026-11-27 it is about 144.6 AU from the Sun.

legs._comment: Heliocentric path built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_voyager.py from JPL Horizons (target -32): Lambert legs between real positions; planet tours spliced in; ends where the craft passes 54.514 AU (1.1 x Pluto's aphelion), the edge of the Solar System view for now.

Jupiter tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -32, 1979-07-06 -> 1979-07-13): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.

Saturn tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -32, 1981-08-22 -> 1981-08-29): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 1 d.

Uranus tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -32, 1986-01-21 -> 1986-01-28): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 8 d.

Neptune tour built 2026-11-27 by tools/build_planet_tour.py from JPL Horizons (target -32, 1989-08-22 -> 1989-08-29): one planetocentric Lambert arc per piece between real periapses, moon flybys (pinned to the moon's modeled position) and filler waypoints keeping each piece under 60 deg / 8 d.
1998-04-09T23:00:00Z: crosses 54.514 AU from the Sun (Horizons, hourly); the Solar System view stops the path here, and the heliosphere layer carries it on.
